shots.phrase: Begin by framing Introduction to Algorithm Analysis as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results.
Consider this worked case: A sorting algorithm must guarantee that the output array contains all input elements in non-decreasing order.
List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion.
Now define Asymptotic Notation Basics precisely enough that another learner could test the definition.
Consider this worked case: Big-O notation for a nested loop sorting algorithm indicates quadratic time complexity, O(n^2), as input size doubles.
Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them.
With the foundation in place, examine how Loop Invariants for Correctness operates in a concrete sequence.
Consider this worked case: In a linear search, the invariant states that the target element, if present, must be in the unexamined portion of the array.
Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition.
Next, compare the choices involved in Divide-and-Conquer Strategy and make the decision criteria explicit.
Consider this worked case: Merge sort divides an array into halves, recursively sorts each half, and merges the sorted subarrays into a single ordered array.
Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts.
Apply Recurrence Relations to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition.
Consider this worked case: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) describes the time complexity of merge sort, solved via the Master Theorem.
Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step.
Examine the tradeoffs in Graph Representation, including what improves and what becomes more difficult.
Consider this worked case: An adjacency list for a directed graph stores each vertex followed by a list of its outgoing edges, enabling efficient neighbor lookups.
State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable.
Stress-test the reasoning around Graph Traversal Methods with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome.
Consider this worked case: Breadth-first search explores all vertices at a given depth before moving to the next level, ensuring the shortest path in unweighted graphs.
Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds.
Use Data Structure Selection to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action.
Consider this worked case: Choosing a hash table over a linked list for key-value storage reduces lookup time from O(n) to O(1) average case, provided a good collision strategy is used.
Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause.
Connect Algorithm Design Process to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system.
Consider this worked case: Before coding, a developer specifies the input array and expected sorted output, verifies correctness via trace, and calculates O(n log n) time and O(n) space requirements.
Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations.
Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis.

Consider this worked case: The checklist confirms that the loop invariant holds, asymptotic bounds are calculated, and graph traversal uses the appropriate adjacency structure for the problem constraints.
For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step.
